reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
clinicalPearls: Cavernous haemangioma is the commonest benign tumour of the liver, usually discovered incidentally on imaging performed for other reasons.
It is more frequent in women and may enlarge under oestrogenic influence such as pregnancy or exogenous hormones.
The great majority are small, solitary and asymptomatic and require no intervention.
Large or giant lesions can cause capsular stretch pain, early satiety and mass effect on adjacent organs.
The imaging hallmark is peripheral, nodular, discontinuous contrast enhancement with progressive centripetal fill-in, and MRI shows a markedly T2-hyperintense light-bulb lesion.
Percutaneous biopsy is generally contraindicated because of bleeding risk and is rarely needed given the characteristic imaging appearances.
Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon, a consumptive coagulopathy with thrombocytopenia, is a rare complication of very large lesions.
Resection, enucleation or arterial embolisation is reserved for symptomatic lesions, diagnostic uncertainty, rapid growth or complications.
reference.pathophysiology: Hepatic haemangiomas are benign vascular malformations rather than true neoplasms, composed of multiple large, thin-walled, blood-filled vascular channels lined by a single layer of flat endothelium and separated by fibrous septa. They are thought to be congenital in origin, arising from a hamartomatous malformation of vascular tissue that enlarges by ectasia rather than by cellular hyperplasia. Blood flow through the lesion is slow, predisposing to intralesional thrombosis, fibrosis and occasionally calcification over time. Their tendency to grow during pregnancy and with oestrogen exposure implicates hormonal sensitivity of the vascular stroma. Very large lesions can sequester platelets and consume clotting factors within their sluggish vascular spaces, producing the Kasabach-Merritt consumptive coagulopathy, and their thin walls may rarely rupture to cause haemorrhage.
additionalDifferentials: Hypervascular hepatic metastases such as neuroendocrine deposits
additionalInvestigations: MRI with T2-weighted and dynamic contrast sequences
Labelled red-cell scintigraphy in equivocal cases
Full blood count and coagulation screen if a giant lesion is present
Serum alpha-fetoprotein to help exclude malignancy
redFlags: Sudden severe abdominal pain with hypotension suggesting rupture and haemoperitoneum
Rapidly enlarging lesion on serial imaging
Unexplained thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy indicating Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon
Diagnostic uncertainty where malignancy cannot be excluded
reference.prognosis: The outlook is excellent for the typical small, stable lesion, which needs no treatment, and even large lesions have a favourable prognosis after resection, with spontaneous rupture being rare.
pitfalls: Proceeding to percutaneous biopsy of a suspected haemangioma and causing haemorrhage.
Mislabelling a hypervascular metastasis or hepatocellular carcinoma as a benign haemangioma.
Attributing unrelated abdominal symptoms to a small incidental haemangioma.
Underestimating coagulopathy risk before intervening on a giant lesion.

management: Reassure and simply observe the typical small, asymptomatic lesion, which needs no treatment or routine follow-up
Reserve intervention such as surgical enucleation or resection for large or giant lesions causing pain, mass effect, or complications
Consider transarterial embolisation to control symptoms, reduce lesion size, or manage rupture
Manage Kasabach-Merritt consumptive coagulopathy in giant lesions with blood-product support and definitive treatment of the lesion
Avoid percutaneous biopsy because of bleeding risk, relying on characteristic imaging for diagnosis
Counsel on possible enlargement with oestrogen exposure or pregnancy and monitor large lesions accordingly
